newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU companies urge "hands off" new services.
newsitem.headline: EU companies urge "hands off" new services.

text.p: Some of Europe's top media and telecommunications companies plan to urge the European Union later this month to take a "hands off" approach to regulating the Internet and other new electronic services.

"New services require a fresh regulatory approach," says a draft report expected to be endorsed by a group that was set up to advise the European Commission and includes the heads of companies such as Olivetti, Bertelsmann and BBC Broadcasting.
"Existing telecommunications and traditional broadcasting regulations are not appropriate," it says.

The report, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, also asks the EU to strengthen its efforts to open up telecoms markets to competition by setting up a committee of national regulators to coordinate activities and possibly an arbitration body to resolve disputes between companies.
"The concept is that in a market based on free competition, arbitration is the best way to prevent abuse of a dominant position," said an official from one of the companies represented on the group.
The group decided it was premature, however, to consider setting up a European telecoms regulatory authority.

The Commission asked the executives from about 30 companies -- including IBM, British Telecom and Polygram International -- to propose ways to ensure that the EU takes full advantage of the "information society", or the revolution in media, telecoms and computer technologies.
The language on new services and telecoms was drafted by a working group on regulatory issues, headed by Carlo De Benedetti, honorary chairman of Italian computer and telecoms company Olivetti.
It is likely to be finalised at a meeting between working group heads set for February 23, the industry official said.

The draft report reflects the fear that the EU will apply its rules in areas such as telecoms licensing and public service obligations or quotas on non-EU television content to new broadcast and online computer services.
France has, for example, led a campaign to apply quotas to new broadcast services.
The report says the new regime should be based on competition law -- that is, rules barring abuse of a dominant position or anti-competitive agreements between companies.
The new services should not be subject to more restrictive regulation than other service and products, for example in the area of defamation laws, it adds.
Nor should they be subject to new tax schemes, which would inhibit their growth and divert them to non-EU jurisdictions.
The companies say the EU needs to strengthen intellectual property rights for the new services, along with protection of encrypted services and recognition of electronic signatures.
In the telecoms sector, they highlight the need to ensure that the EU's plan to abolish state telecoms monopolies in most countries by January 1, 1998, is enforced.

Noting that most countries have been late in implementing existing rules, the report says the Commission should spend more time auditing the situation and issue detailed guidelines telling regulators and industry how to implement EU laws.
